author: Gabriel Scotto
title: Athens County Commission: Activists concerned about use of cameras by county law enforcement - NewsBreak
text:
By Gabriel Scotto ,
1 days ago
A group of concerned citizens appeared at the Athens County Board of Commissioners to discuss the use of Flock Safety cameras in Athens County.
Athens County has 10 Flock Safety cameras, which are solar-powered and motion-activated. These cameras can be used to record license plate numbers and vehicle details such as the make and model.
Data from these cameras can be used by law enforcement to find missing persons, stolen vehicles and monitor human traffickers, Rodney Smith, the Athens County Sheriff, said.
Athens County received a federal grant to pay for a subscription to Flock Safety’s services, worth around $3,000 per camera per year.
Activist groups such as the ACLU of Ohio have expressed concern about Flock Safety cameras, including potential infringements upon civil liberties and data security.
The organization held a town hall meeting at the Athens Community Center on June 10 to educate the public about the privacy concerns surrounding Flock Safety cameras.
A group of activists affiliated with the ACLU of Ohio circulated a petition throughout Athens County, opposing the renewal of the county’s contract with Flock Safety.
This petition was presented to the commissioners, but the activists were informed the contract with Flock Safety had already been renewed and it was too late to back out, Lenny Eliason, the president of the Athens County Board of Commissioners, explained.
However, in light of the concerns expressed by the petitioners, Eliason said Athens County will look into alternatives to Flock Safety’s services in future.
Most of those present at the commissioner’s meeting were concerned about what Flock Safety could potentially do with the data it collected from the 10 cameras in Athens County.
Among the concerns expressed by activists to the commissioners were the use of data for training artificial intelligence and the use of data by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in its immigration raids.
Other concerns included the fact the cameras themselves were installed in Athens County without public hearings or input, according to one activist.
Smith reassured the petitioners that the Athens County Sheriff’s Office wouldn’t make use of Flock Safety’s services if it was not confident that the data from these cameras wouldn’t be used for nefarious purposes.
“I’m skeptical. I look at evidence, I look at facts and if I thought for one second that Flock was doing anything that went against my beliefs or that goes against how I protect the citizens of Athens County, I wouldn’t use them,” Smith explained.
In other news, the commissioners authorized Athens County Emergency Medical Services (ACEMS) to purchase a brand new ambulance from Penn Care, Inc. of Niles for $358,204.
The new ambulance will be different from ACEMS’ existing fleet of ambulances in that it would be based on a pickup truck chassis rather than a van chassis. Specifically, a Ford F-550 Super Duty chassis.
While this increases the upfront cost, it reduces long term costs because the ambulance body is separate from the chassis and can therefore be replaced in future without being forced to retire the whole vehicle, Assistant Chief Randy Crossen, the director of operations at ACEMS, said.
Along with being based on a pickup truck chassis rather than a van chassis, the new ambulance would be powered by gasoline rather than diesel fuel. As a result, maintenance costs for the new ambulance will be cheaper than those of ACEMS’ existing fleet, Crossen explained.
The commissioners also spoke with Nick Tepe, the vice chair of the Hockhocking Adena Bikeway Advisory Committee, about a proposal to post speed limits along the bike path.
There have not been any efforts to place a speed limit on the bike path until now because of the difficulty of enforcing a speed limit.
Unfortunately, a growing number of incidents involving near collisions between cyclists and pedestrians has forced the advisory committee to consider taking such action, Tepe said.
While some of these incidents have involved conventional bicycles, many of them have involved people riding on non-permitted e-bikes.
State law only permits e-bikes with a maximum speed of 20 miles per hour to travel on sidewalks and bike paths.
By placing a speed limit on the bike path, people will be encouraged to obey the rules and to call out dangerous behavior, Tepe explained.
Eliason was opposed to the idea of placing a speed limit on the bike path on the grounds that it could lead to “overzealous” people trying to enforce the rules and that putting out a speed limit creates the expectation of enforcement by officers of the law.
Charlie Adkins, the vice president of the Athens County Board of Commissioners, suggested holding discussions with the sheriff’s office about what could be done to ensure people practice safe behavior on the bike path.
In other news, the commissioners received an update from Otis Crockron, the executive director of Athens County Children Services (ACCS) , about the progress made on its new building.
The 27,500 square foot structure replaces four older structures at the ACCS’ main campus at 18 Stonybrook Drive. The total cost of the project is estimated at $12.9 million, as previously reported by The Messenger.
As of June, the project is $140,000 under budget and substantial completion of the building is expected to take place on Oct. 19.
Initial plans were for ACCS to move into the new building by mid-November, though it is likely that move-in will not take place until early December, Crockron explained.
The next Athens County Commissioners meeting will be held on Tuesday, July 23 at 9:30 a.m. in the commissioner’s conference room, located on the second-floor annex of the Athens County Courthouse at 15 S. Court St.

Activist groups such as the ACLU of Ohio have expressed concern about Flock Safety cameras, including potential infringements upon civil liberties and data security. The organization held a town hall meeting at the Athens Community Center on June 10 to educate the public about the privacy concerns surrounding Flock Safety cameras.
